2. The description summarizes its purpose.
3. Search systems may choose other snippets; metadata should describe actual visible content rather than promise unsupported features.
hints: Use standard metadata elements.
Which attribute names the description field?

questions.question: When adding JSON-LD to a product page, what makes the structured data trustworthy and safe to embed?
questions.correctAnswer: It should describe the actual visible product and current facts. Serialize data and escape unsafe HTML-significant content before embedding it in a script. Validate the vocabulary and avoid claims the page does not support.
questions.explanation: Valid JSON alone does not guarantee safe HTML embedding or accurate structured data. JSON-LD is a machine-readable description, not a shortcut to guaranteed rich results.
hints: Separate semantic accuracy from embedding safety.
Could a value contain a closing script sequence?

questions.question: How should SSR versus CSR be evaluated for a public content page’s discoverability?
questions.correctAnswer: Server-rendered HTML exposes meaningful initial content without waiting for client execution. CSR can still be processed by capable crawlers but adds rendering dependencies and delays. Preserve semantic content, valid links and metadata whichever rendering model is chosen.
questions.explanation: SSR alone does not guarantee indexing or good rankings. Authentication, robots rules, canonicalization and content quality remain separate concerns.
hints: Compare what arrives in the first response.
Does meaningful content require client execution?

questions.question: A page becomes slower after repeatedly opening and closing a panel. What memory evidence should you collect?
questions.correctAnswer: Repeat the same interaction and compare heap snapshots after cleanup opportunities. Inspect retained detached DOM nodes and their retaining paths. Look for listeners, timers, observers or caches that keep disposed resources reachable.
questions.explanation: A temporary allocation spike is not necessarily a leak. The useful signal is persistent growth tied to resources that should have been released.
hints: Find what remains reachable.
Which owner retains a supposedly disposed node?

questions.question: Why can good local Lighthouse results coexist with poor field Core Web Vitals?
questions.correctAnswer: Lab tests run under a controlled scenario. Field data reflects real devices, networks and user interactions across visits. Compare like-for-like conditions and investigate the actual field distribution.
questions.explanation: One fast local run does not represent all users. Some interaction and long-session layout problems may not occur during a short synthetic test.
hints: Population and scenario differ.
What user behavior does the lab run omit?

questions.question: Which set gives the good Core Web Vitals thresholds assessed at the 75th percentile?

options.text: All three must equal zero on every visit.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.explanation: The thresholds cover loading, responsiveness and stability. Averages can hide poor experiences, so the percentile criterion matters.
hints: Match each metric’s unit.
CLS is unitless, unlike time metrics.

questions.question: A click handler performs 300 ms of CPU work before updating the screen. What changes can reduce interaction latency?
questions.correctAnswer: Reduce unnecessary computation first. Move suitable heavy computation to a worker or split it into yielding tasks. Provide prompt feedback and measure the resulting interaction rather than only total throughput.
questions.explanation: A microtask loop does not necessarily yield to rendering. Deferring all work without considering feedback can merely move the same visible delay.
hints: The main thread cannot paint while occupied.
Where can work yield or run elsewhere?

questions.question: Why is this custom control not an accessible replacement for a button, and what is the simplest correction?
questions.code: Save
questions.correctAnswer: role alone does not add focus or keyboard behavior. Replace it with: <button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>.
questions.explanation:
1. The div exposes a role but is not natively keyboard-focusable.
2. It lacks standard Enter/Space activation.
3. A native button supplies those behaviors; styling can preserve the desired appearance.
hints: Semantics do not implement interaction.
Can a keyboard user reach and activate it?

questions.question: For a composite toolbar, how does roving tabindex reduce tab stops while retaining keyboard access?
questions.correctAnswer: Give one current item tabindex=0 and the others tabindex=-1. Use the pattern’s arrow-key behavior to move focus and update that current item. Tab enters or leaves the composite instead of visiting every control.
questions.explanation: The keyboard pattern must match the widget role and orientation. Simply setting all items to -1 makes the toolbar unreachable.
hints: Separate entry into the widget from movement within it.
Which item is the single tab stop?

questions.question: Follow-up to PAS-003: why should CLS testing continue after the first screen appears?
questions.correctAnswer: Unexpected shifts can occur during later interactions and loading. Ads, fonts and dynamically inserted content can move existing elements. Measure representative page lifetimes and distinguish expected interaction-related exclusions from unrelated shifts.
questions.explanation: A stable initial screenshot does not prove long-session stability. CLS uses defined session-window and recent-input rules, not a simple count of all movement.
hints: Layout changes continue after load.
Which late content can displace existing UI?

questions.question: What makes a React component’s render function pure?
questions.correctAnswer: Its output depends on its inputs. It does not mutate preexisting external state during render. Repeating render with the same inputs should not produce new observable side effects.
questions.explanation: React may render more than once or abandon work. Network requests and external mutations during render therefore have no reliable commit lifecycle.
hints: Rendering may be repeated.
Would replaying the function change the outside world?

questions.question: Which JSX passes a handler to run on click rather than invoking it during render?
questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: React expects a function for onClick. Calling save() while producing JSX runs it immediately; returning another function would be a different explicit contract.
hints: Pass behavior, not its result.
Where are the call parentheses?

questions.question: Why might this name edit fail to update the UI, and which setter call fixes it?
questions.code:
user.name = "Ada";
setUser(user);
questions.correctAnswer: It reuses the mutated state object. Use: setUser(previous => ({ ...previous, name: "Ada" }));
questions.explanation:
1. The assignment mutates the current snapshot.
2. The setter receives the same object identity and may be skipped.
3. An immutable replacement communicates the change without corrupting prior snapshots.
hints: State is a snapshot.
Is the next object a new identity?

questions.question: Why does reading count immediately after setCount(count + 1) still see the old count in that handler?
questions.correctAnswer: The handler belongs to one render’s snapshot. The setter queues a later state update. It does not rewrite the local count binding in the running handler.
questions.explanation: A setter is not synchronous assignment to a local variable. Compute the intended next value locally when that same handler needs it.
hints: A render creates local bindings.
Can a setter rewrite an existing closure?

questions.question: Starting at zero, this click only adds one. Correct it to add three using queued updates.
questions.correctAnswer: Each call replaces state with the same snapshot-derived value. Replace each call with: setCount(previous => previous + 1);
questions.explanation:
1. All three expressions read the same count.
2. React queues three replacements with 1.
3. Functional updaters consume the preceding queued value, producing 1, 2 and 3. Keep updater functions pure.
hints: Look at each queued value.
Can each update receive the latest pending state?

questions.question: A child needs to change its parent’s selectedId. Which approach follows React’s data flow?

options.text: Call a callback prop supplied by the parent.
Change a destructured selectedId local variable.
Store the new value on the JSX element object.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: The parent owns its state and passes data down. Mutating a prop or assigning to a local parameter does not request a parent update.
hints: Find the state owner.
How can a child request a change?

questions.question: Rows keep the wrong local input state after reordering. Correct the key choice.
questions.correctAnswer: Index keys associate state with positions. Use: <Row key={item.id} item={item} />;
questions.explanation:
1. React matches siblings by type and key.
2. Reordering with index keys preserves positional identities.
3. Stable record IDs let state follow the corresponding records; keys must be unique among siblings.
hints: Keys identify logical items.
Does position remain stable after reorder?

questions.question: How do React’s render and commit phases differ?
questions.correctAnswer: Render calculates the next UI description. Commit applies the necessary host changes. Effects synchronize external systems in relation to committed work, not every attempted render.
questions.explanation: A render can be restarted or discarded. Treating every component call as a DOM update confuses calculation with committed changes.
hints: Separate calculation from application.
Can calculated work be abandoned?

questions.question: Write a complete NameField component with state-controlled text and an associated visible label.
questions.explanation:
1. Initialize the value as a string.
2. Each change copies the input value into state.
3. The next render controls the input and useId connects its label. Do not switch the value between undefined and a string.
hints: The value must have one owner.
Pair value with a change handler.

questions.question: A form should let the DOM own an input after giving it an initial name. Which React prop fits, and how is it read on submit?
questions.correctAnswer: Use defaultValue for the initial text. Read the submitted field through FormData or a ref. Changing defaultValue later is not the controlled-input update model.
questions.explanation: value makes the field controlled and needs appropriate updates. defaultValue establishes initial content without continuously owning the current value.
hints: Initial and current values differ.
Which prop specifies only initialization?

questions.question: Why does an empty list display 0, and what fixes the condition?
questions.code:
return
{items.length && }
;
questions.correctAnswer: The && expression returns numeric zero. Use: {items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />};
questions.explanation:
1. When length is zero, && evaluates to zero.
2. React renders numeric zero as text.
3. A boolean comparison produces false, which React omits.
hints: && returns an operand.
Is zero omitted like false?

questions.question: Where should an ordinary useState call appear?

options.text: Inside a conditional after an early return.
Inside a loop whose length depends on props.
At the top level of a component or custom Hook.

questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: React tracks ordinary Hooks by consistent call order. Conditional calls and loops can change that order between renders; event callbacks are not component renders.
hints: Hook order must be stable.
Could this location run a different number of times?

questions.question: How do event.stopPropagation and event.preventDefault differ in a React click handler?
questions.correctAnswer: stopPropagation stops further propagation of that event. preventDefault cancels its cancelable default action. Neither operation is a substitute for the other.
questions.explanation: A link can still navigate after propagation is stopped. Preventing navigation does not necessarily stop parent click handlers.
hints: Separate listeners from browser behavior.
Is navigation a listener or a default action?

questions.question: Write a complete controlled checkbox component labeled Subscribe, initially unchecked.
questions.explanation:
1. Control checked with a boolean.
2. Read event.target.checked on each change.
3. Using value would read the submission value rather than the checked state.
hints: Checkboxes have a dedicated boolean property.
Which event target field reflects selection?

questions.question: Two sibling filters must show the same selection. Where should that shared state live?
questions.correctAnswer: Move it to their closest appropriate common owner. Pass the current selection and change callbacks to both. Keep a single source of truth for the shared value.
questions.explanation: Duplicated sibling state needs synchronization and can drift. Lifting everything globally is unnecessary when a nearby owner can coordinate it.
hints: Locate the common owner.
Can both children receive the same value?

questions.question: A Row receives key={item.id}. How should it also receive that ID for use inside Row?
questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: React uses key for reconciliation and does not forward it as a normal prop. A separate prop communicates the data explicitly.
hints: Some JSX attributes are special.
Does reconciliation metadata reach props?

questions.question: An editor should discard its draft when the selected document changes. How can a key express that behavior?
questions.correctAnswer: Render the editor with key={documentId}. A different key makes React treat it as a different component instance. Its local state resets instead of being preserved at that position.
questions.explanation: Changing ordinary props does not inherently reset state. A key reset also resets other state and effects in that subtree, so the boundary should be deliberate.
hints: State belongs to tree identity.
What happens when identity changes?

questions.question: Why does this expensive initializer run on every render, and what is the corrected Hook call?
questions.code: const [items, setItems] = useState(buildItems());
questions.correctAnswer: The function is called before useState receives its argument. Use: const [items, setItems] = useState(buildItems);
questions.explanation:
1. JavaScript evaluates buildItems() on every component call.
2. Passing the function lets React invoke it for initialization.
3. Development Strict Mode may invoke the initializer twice to check purity.
hints: Inspect argument evaluation.
Can the Hook receive a function instead of its result?

questions.question: Why might a reusable Card accept children instead of hard-coding a particular form inside it?
questions.correctAnswer: children lets callers supply nested content. Card can own the shared visual structure. The content remains composed by the caller rather than selected by a growing list of special-case props.
questions.explanation: Composition separates the wrapper’s responsibility from the content’s behavior. children is still ordinary React data and does not imply independent state sharing.
hints: Separate container and content.
What should the caller choose?

questions.question: Which task most clearly belongs in an Effect?

options.text: Concatenating firstName and lastName for display.
Sorting a copied array for rendering.
Computing whether a supplied list is empty.
Connecting a component to an external chat subscription.

questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: An Effect synchronizes with an external system and can return cleanup. Deriving display text from props usually belongs in render; user-triggered operations often belong in their event handler.
hints: Identify the external system.
Does work need to track mounting and dependencies?

questions.question: This input starts uncontrolled and later becomes controlled. What should its initialization be when it always represents text?
questions.code:
const [name, setName] = useState();
return <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />;
questions.correctAnswer: Initialize with an empty string: const [name, setName] = useState("");
questions.explanation:
1. An undefined value does not establish a controlled text value.
2. After typing, a string switches the ownership mode.
3. Start with a string and keep the value a string throughout the component lifetime.
hints: Keep input ownership consistent.
What empty value still has type string?

questions.question: When should a timer handle live in a ref instead of state?
questions.correctAnswer: Use a ref when changing the handle should not affect rendered output. The ref persists across renders. Updating its current field does not schedule a render.
questions.explanation: State is for values whose changes should drive the UI. A ref is mutable storage, so reading arbitrary current values during render can undermine predictable rendering.
hints: Does this value affect the UI?
Should assigning it cause a render?

questions.question: Write a complete Toggle component whose button alternates between On and Off.
questions.explanation:
1. Initialize the boolean state.
2. The updater negates the pending value.
3. The next render updates text and pressed semantics. The updater stays pure even if invoked again in development.
hints: The next value depends on the previous one.
Use a functional state update.

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-007: must a record key be globally unique across every list on the page?
questions.correctAnswer: No, keys need to be unique among siblings. The same ID may appear in separate lists. Within one sibling set, stable unique keys are needed to match items correctly.
questions.explanation: Keys are interpreted in their parent’s child set. A global key registry is unnecessary and random keys destroy stability.
hints: Identity is contextual.
Which parent compares these children?

questions.question: Why can a pure component appear to render twice in development Strict Mode?
questions.correctAnswer: Strict Mode intentionally repeats selected work to expose impure logic. This is a development check. Fix the impurity instead of relying on an exact render count.
questions.explanation: The extra invocation is not proof that two DOM commits occurred. Production behavior and development diagnostics should not be conflated.
hints: Look for a development-only check.
Is the repeated function supposed to be pure?

questions.question: The subscription keeps using the first roomId. Identify the bug and correct the dependencies.
questions.correctAnswer: roomId is a reactive dependency. Use: }, [roomId]); for the Effect’s closing line.
questions.explanation:
1. The empty list ties the Effect to its initial captured roomId.
2. When roomId changes, no cleanup or reconnect occurs.
3. Including roomId disconnects the old room before connecting the new one.
hints: Effects capture render values.
What change should trigger reconnection?

questions.question: When an Effect dependency changes, in what order do cleanup and setup run?
questions.correctAnswer: React runs the old cleanup using the old captured values. It then runs the new setup using the new values. Final unmount also cleans up the active Effect.
questions.explanation: Cleanup is not limited to unmount. Development Strict Mode can additionally run a setup-cleanup-setup check, so cleanup must undo setup.
hints: Think of replacing one synchronization.
Which subscription must stop first?

questions.question: Replace this Counter with a working component that increments every second and cleans up its timer.
questions.explanation:
1. The original callback captures the initial count.
2. A functional updater reads the pending count instead.
3. Cleanup clears the interval on unmount and during development checks. Timers are not exact clocks.
hints: The callback outlives its render.
Can the setter supply fresh state?

questions.question: Why does this connection restart on every render, and which change removes the unnecessary dependency?
questions.explanation:
1. Dependency comparison uses Object.is.
2. The new object fails identity comparison each render.
3. Moving construction into setup makes roomId the actual reactive input. Do not omit roomId.
hints: Compare object identities.
Where can the setup-only object be created?

questions.question: A component stores fullName in state and updates it in an Effect whenever firstName or lastName changes. How should it be simplified?
questions.correctAnswer: Compute fullName from firstName and lastName during render. Remove the redundant state and synchronization Effect. Memoize only if an actually expensive computation warrants it.
questions.explanation: An Effect creates an avoidable render with stale derived state followed by another render. Pure derivation keeps the value consistent with its inputs.
hints: Can the value be calculated directly?
Is there an external system to synchronize?

questions.question: How does React compare each entry in an Effect dependency list?

options.text: Using JSON.stringify on the entire list.
Using Object.is against the previous entry.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: React does not recursively compare object fields. A fresh array or object can retrigger an Effect even when its contents look identical.
hints: Identity matters for objects.
Which equality algorithm is documented?

questions.question: Write a complete SearchFocus component with an input and a button that focuses it.
questions.explanation:
1. React assigns the committed input node to the ref.
2. The click handler focuses that node.
3. The optional check handles a missing node; manipulating focus during render would be premature.
hints: DOM nodes arrive after commit.
Use the ref in the event handler.

questions.question: Why does useRef(createResource()) still call createResource on every render, and how can predictable one-time initialization avoid that work?
questions.code: const resourceRef = useRef(createResource());
questions.correctAnswer: JavaScript evaluates the argument before calling useRef. Initialize the ref with null and fill current only when it is null. This render-time initialization exception requires a predictable result and no externally observable side effect.
questions.explanation:
1. The component evaluates createResource() on every invocation.
2. useRef keeps only its initial value, so later constructed values are discarded.
3. A guarded initialization avoids repeated work, but pure rendering still matters under development checks.
hints: Check argument evaluation before the Hook runs.
Can the ref start empty and be initialized predictably once?

questions.question: What Hook-order bug appears when enabled changes, and how should the Hook be positioned?
questions.explanation:
1. One render can return without calling the Hook.
2. Another render calls it, changing the Hook sequence.
3. Call Hooks consistently and make returned UI conditional afterward.
hints: Compare both render paths.
Do all paths call the same Hooks?

questions.question: This is ordinary JavaScript using a React-style reducer. What does it log?
questions.explanation:
1. The reducer returns a new state with count increased by amount.
2. The original state is not mutated.
3. The output shows both states. Reducers must remain pure when React invokes them.
hints: Track old and new objects.
Is state assigned to directly?

questions.question: When is useReducer useful compared with several independent useState calls?
questions.correctAnswer: It centralizes related state transitions. Actions describe what happened, and a reducer computes the next state. It is useful when updates must preserve shared invariants across several fields.
questions.explanation: A reducer does not automatically provide global state or improve performance. Independent simple values can remain separate state variables.
hints: Look for coordinated transitions.
Which fields must change together?

questions.question: Why is this reducer unsafe, and what corrected return handles add?
questions.correctAnswer: It mutates the existing state. Use: return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
questions.explanation:
1. The original object is changed before being returned.
2. React may see the same identity and skip work.
3. Immutable calculation preserves previous snapshots and remains safe under repeated purity checks.
hints: The reducer receives a previous snapshot.
Can it construct a new next snapshot?

questions.question: When several providers supply the same context, which value does useContext read?

options.text: The first provider mounted anywhere in the app.
The closest matching provider above the calling component.
The provider returned later by the same component.
An average of every matching provider value.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: Context lookup follows ancestry, not DOM proximity or provider creation order. A provider returned by the same component is below its own Hook call.
hints: Think about the React tree.
Is the provider above the consumer?

questions.question: A context provider creates { user, logout } on every render. What performance concern should you investigate?
questions.correctAnswer: Its value identity changes on every render. Consumers of that context can update even when the meaningful data is unchanged. Consider stable callbacks, memoized values or split contexts after measuring.
questions.explanation: React compares provider values with Object.is. memo on a consumer does not block updates caused by a context it reads.
hints: Inspect the provider value identity.
Can unrelated state recreate the value?

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-038: does createContext(defaultValue) supply defaultValue when an existing provider explicitly supplies undefined?
questions.correctAnswer: No, that provider’s undefined is the value. The default applies only when no matching provider exists above. Validate missing-provider cases separately if the API requires a provider.
questions.explanation: A default value is not a nullish fallback for provider values. Explicit undefined and absent provider are distinct situations.
hints: Distinguish absence from an explicit value.
Was a matching provider found?

questions.question: If two components call the same custom Hook containing useState, do they share its state?
questions.correctAnswer: No, each call has its own state. Custom Hooks share logic. Shared state needs a common owner or an external store.
questions.explanation: Extracting code does not merge Hook instances. Module-level mutable state would be a different mechanism with different lifecycle concerns.
hints: A Hook call is an instance.
How many state owners exist?

questions.question: Implement useToggle(initial = false) returning [value, toggle]. Keep toggle stable across renders.
questions.explanation:
1. Each Hook call owns its own state.
2. The stable callback uses a functional update and captures no changing state.
3. The initial argument initializes once; later initial changes do not reset state.
hints: Avoid capturing the current value.
Can a functional update remove that dependency?

questions.question: What does useMemo cache between renders when its dependencies are unchanged?

options.text: The calculation function’s identity without invoking it.
The result of its calculation function.
All state updates inside the component.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: useMemo calls a calculation and caches its result. useCallback caches a function identity instead. Neither is required for ordinary correctness.
hints: Function versus function result.
Which Hook invokes the calculation?

questions.question: Should every string concatenation in a component be wrapped in useMemo?
questions.correctAnswer: No, cheap calculations usually do not justify it. Measure a real performance problem before adding caching. Prefer simple pure render logic when memoization provides no benefit.
questions.explanation: Memoization adds dependency management and retained values. It is a performance optimization, not a general correctness mechanism.
hints: Compare saved work with overhead.
Is the calculation measurably expensive?

questions.question: Why does this filtered list ignore a changed query, and which dependency list fixes it?
questions.correctAnswer: query is captured but omitted. Use: [items, query].
questions.explanation:
1. The cache stays valid according to the incomplete list.
2. Changing only query reuses the old result.
3. Include every reactive input to the calculation; mutating items in place is a separate identity problem.
hints: List all values read by the calculation.
Which one can change independently?

questions.question: What can still render a memoized component even when its props compare equal?
questions.correctAnswer: Its own state updates can render it. Changes to context it consumes can also render it. memo is an optimization and is not a guarantee that rendering never occurs.
questions.explanation: memo primarily compares props from a parent. It does not freeze the component or detach it from state and context.
hints: Props are not the only input.
What does the component subscribe to?

questions.question: A memoized child rerenders because its parent passes a fresh callback. When might useCallback help?
questions.correctAnswer: It can preserve the callback identity while its dependencies are unchanged. That can let the child’s prop comparison succeed. It helps only if other props and consumed context are also sufficiently stable.
questions.explanation: Caching a callback does not stop the parent from rendering. An always-new object prop can still defeat the child’s memoization.
hints: Examine all compared props.
Is the callback the actual changing input?

questions.question: Assume loadData and setData have stable identities. Why is this async Effect setup invalid, and how should asynchronous work be started with cleanup?
questions.explanation:
1. React invokes setup and expects undefined or a cleanup function.
2. An async function always returns a Promise.
3. Keep cancellation or stale-result protection in synchronous cleanup; handle promise rejection inside the async work.
hints: Check what async functions return.
Can cleanup be returned synchronously?

questions.question: When can useLayoutEffect be justified over useEffect?
questions.correctAnswer: Use it for layout measurement that must affect the UI before the browser paints. It runs after DOM changes and blocks repaint while it works. Prefer useEffect when that blocking timing is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Using layout Effects for general fetching does not make network work synchronous. Excessive blocking work delays visible updates.
hints: Ask whether a visible intermediate layout is acceptable.
Must measurement happen before paint?

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-025: a development setup-cleanup-setup cycle creates duplicate connections. What should be fixed?
questions.correctAnswer: Make cleanup fully undo the connection created by setup. Each setup should own the resource it returns cleanup for. After replay, only the currently active connection should remain.
questions.explanation: A ref guard that merely skips the second setup hides missing cleanup and can break real remounts. The lifecycle must remain correct under replacement.
hints: Track resource ownership.
Does each setup have a matching teardown?

questions.question: In React 19, how can a function component receive a ref from its parent?

options.text: Convert the component to a class.
Accept ref as a prop and pass it to the intended node or use it in useImperativeHandle.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: React 19 supports ref as a prop for function components. A new component does not need forwardRef solely to receive it.
hints: Use the current function-component API.
Which prop now carries the reference?

questions.question: Write FocusInput accepting ref and exposing only focus(), while keeping its DOM ref internal.
questions.explanation:
1. Keep the DOM node in a private ref.
2. Expose a narrow handle through useImperativeHandle.
3. The parent can focus without receiving every DOM operation. Prefer declarative props when they express the interaction.
hints: Separate the public handle from the DOM node.
Which Hook customizes the ref value?

questions.question: Why is generating list keys this way invalid, and what should replace the expression?
questions.correctAnswer: useId cannot be called in this loop and is not a data-key generator. Use: <Row key={item.id} item={item} />;
questions.explanation:
1. The loop can change Hook call count.
2. useId is intended for accessibility relationships, not record identity.
3. Stable IDs from the data preserve list identity.
hints: Separate accessibility IDs from data IDs.
Can list length change Hook order?

questions.question: Why use useId for label and input relationships instead of incrementing a module-level counter during render?
questions.correctAnswer: useId coordinates IDs across server rendering and hydration. A mutable counter depends on render order and replay. The server and client component trees still need to match.
questions.explanation: A random or order-dependent ID can differ between server and client. useId solves identity generation for relationships, not mismatched application structure.
hints: Server and client must agree.
Could rendering occur in a different order?

questions.question: A text field loses its draft whenever its parent rerenders. The child component function is declared inside that parent. Why?
questions.correctAnswer: Each parent render creates a new component function identity. React treats it as a different component type at that position. Move the child definition to module scope and pass inputs as props.
questions.explanation: Stable JSX position is not enough when the component type changes. Memoizing unrelated data does not fix the type identity problem.
hints: Component type participates in identity.
Is the function object stable between renders?

questions.question: Run these pure reducer calls. What is logged?
questions.explanation:
1. The first add produces count 2.
2. reset replaces it with zero.
3. The final add produces 5. Dispatch order matters; actions are not merged as object patches.
hints: Apply actions in order.
Does reset add or replace?

questions.question: Why should submitting an order usually happen in the submit handler rather than an Effect watching a submitted flag?
questions.correctAnswer: The submission is caused by a specific interaction. The handler has the event’s relevant data and intent. An Effect introduces synchronization that can replay or become detached from that intent.
questions.explanation: Effects are appropriate when keeping an external system synchronized with rendering. They are not a default replacement for event handlers.
hints: Identify the cause of the work.
Is it an interaction or ongoing synchronization?

questions.question: A portal renders outside its parent’s DOM subtree. Where do React events propagate?

options.text: Only through the portal’s physical DOM ancestors, with no React ancestry.
They never propagate from a portal.
They always propagate to every React root.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: Portals change physical DOM placement without changing React ancestry. Context and React event propagation follow the React tree.
hints: There are two trees.
Which tree owns the React relationship?

questions.question: Typing in a search field rerenders a large unrelated dashboard. What structural change should be considered before memoizing every child?
questions.correctAnswer: Move the input state closer to the input where possible. Keep unrelated expensive content outside that frequently updated subtree. Lift only the state that other consumers actually need.
questions.explanation: State placement controls which component begins the update. Broad memoization can add complexity without addressing unnecessarily high ownership.
hints: Inspect the state owner.
Which subtree truly needs every keystroke?

questions.question: Why can this custom comparator leave the child calling an outdated handler?
questions.correctAnswer:
The custom comparison ignores a callback that may capture changed state. Remove it and use the default prop comparison.

const Row = memo(RowView);
questions.explanation:
1. Returning true permits reuse of the prior render.
2. The old onSelect can retain old parent state.
3. A comparator must preserve equivalent behavior, not just equivalent labels.
hints: Function props carry closures.
Can equal text hide a changed callback?

questions.question: Does automatic batching mean React merges every user interaction into one update?
questions.correctAnswer: No, batching groups updates within supported scheduling contexts. Separate intentional user events are handled separately. React preserves event-level behavior such as disabling a button before a later click.
questions.explanation: Batching reduces intermediate renders but does not erase interaction boundaries. Do not depend on an exact render count as a correctness condition.
hints: Distinct events carry distinct intent.
Could the next click need the committed result?

questions.question: Why use useSyncExternalStore instead of a hand-written Effect to read a mutable external store during concurrent rendering?
questions.correctAnswer: It provides a defined snapshot-and-subscription contract. React can detect changes around rendering and keep the view consistent. Supply a server snapshot as well when server rendering requires it.
questions.explanation: An Effect subscribes after rendering and can miss consistency requirements. The snapshot must remain stable while the store has not changed.
hints: A store can change outside React.
How does React validate the snapshot it rendered?

questions.question: What is wrong with returning a fresh object from every getSnapshot call?
questions.explanation:
1. React compares snapshots by Object.is.
2. A fresh object always appears changed.
3. That can cause repeated renders; mutating one cached object without changing identity is also incorrect.
hints: Snapshot identity is a change signal.
Does unchanged data return an unchanged identity?

questions.question: What failures should a React error boundary be expected to catch?
questions.correctAnswer: It catches rendering errors in its descendant component tree. It shows a fallback instead of the failed subtree. It does not generally catch event-handler errors or arbitrary asynchronous callback failures.
questions.explanation: A boundary does not replace try/catch in event-driven async workflows. It also cannot recover its own failing fallback by catching itself.
hints: Locate the failure phase.
Did it happen while rendering descendants?

questions.question: Where should boundaries be placed on a dashboard with independent panels?
questions.correctAnswer: Place them around useful recovery regions. A failed panel can then show a local fallback while other panels remain usable. Keep a broader boundary for failures outside those regions.
questions.explanation: One boundary around every tiny element creates noisy recovery behavior. One app-wide boundary can unnecessarily remove healthy parts of the interface.
hints: Choose a meaningful failure region.
What can remain useful after one panel fails?

questions.question: What must a promise returned by a React lazy loader resolve to?

options.text: An object whose default property is a valid component type.
A callback that directly mutates the root element.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: React lazy uses the resolved default export as the component. A named export can be adapted explicitly, but returning an arbitrary JSX element is not the module contract.
hints: Think about a module namespace.
Which export does lazy consume?

questions.question: Why can this lazy component reset state, and where should its declaration move?
questions.explanation:
1. Each parent render creates a new lazy component object.
2. React may treat it as a different type and reset state.
3. A stable module-level declaration also avoids redefining the loader wrapper.
hints: Component type must remain stable.
Where can the lazy declaration run once?

questions.question: Write a complete module that lazily imports a default-exported Reports component and shows Loading reports while it loads.
questions.explanation:
1. The lazy loader begins when React first tries to render Reports.
2. Suspense displays the fallback while the import is pending.
3. A rejected import needs an error boundary; Suspense handles waiting, not the final error fallback.
hints: The loading boundary surrounds the lazy child.
Keep the component type outside render.

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-020: can a server render rely on an Effect to fetch content before generating its initial HTML?
questions.correctAnswer: No, Effects do not run during server rendering. Use the framework’s server data-loading mechanism for initial server content. Client Effects can synchronize after the client commits.
questions.explanation: An Effect-based fetch leaves initial server output without that fetched result. Hydration does not retroactively change what the server initially sent.
hints: Check where Effects execute.
Has a client commit happened on the server?

questions.question: How can a React 19 callback ref clean up an external registration associated with a DOM node?
questions.correctAnswer: Register the node when the callback receives it. Return a cleanup function that removes that registration. Keep setup and cleanup symmetric, including development checks.
questions.explanation: Returning cleanup gives the ref its own lifecycle. An implicit return of an unrelated value is not a cleanup contract.
hints: Refs can own imperative resources.
What reverses the registration?

questions.question: Does putting an Effect-based fetch inside Suspense automatically show the boundary’s fallback?
questions.correctAnswer: No, arbitrary fetching in Effects does not activate Suspense. The rendered subtree must use a Suspense-enabled source such as lazy or a supported promise-reading integration. Use framework-supported data loading rather than inventing unsupported suspension contracts.
questions.explanation: Suspense observes rendering that suspends. A loading boolean changed after an Effect is a separate UI mechanism.
hints: Suspension must be visible during render.
Does the Effect throw or read a supported pending resource during render?

questions.question: A page has a slow recommendations panel and a fast article. How should Suspense boundaries be arranged for progressive reveal?
questions.correctAnswer: Keep the article outside the slow panel’s boundary. Wrap recommendations with a meaningful local fallback. Add nested boundaries only where separate reveal stages improve the experience.
questions.explanation: One outer boundary can delay all children together. Excessive tiny boundaries can create distracting loading fragmentation.
hints: Group content that should appear together.
Which section should not wait for recommendations?

questions.question: Which update should remain urgent when a text input also triggers an expensive result view?

options.text: The state controlling the input’s current text.
Every update, including the input value, must be transitioned.
Only analytics counters must remain urgent.
No update can be urgent once useTransition is used.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.explanation: Transition updates cannot control a text input’s immediate value reliably. Keep typing responsive and transition or defer the expensive dependent work.
hints: Typing has immediate feedback requirements.
Which value directly controls the input?

questions.question: What does marking a state update as a Transition change?
questions.correctAnswer: It marks the resulting rendering work as non-urgent. React can interrupt that work for more urgent updates. It does not make synchronous JavaScript inside the callback run on another thread.
questions.explanation: Wrapping an expensive synchronous calculation in startTransition does not make the calculation itself nonblocking. The scheduling benefit concerns React rendering updates.
hints: Separate JavaScript execution from render scheduling.
Is there a worker involved?

questions.question: Under the documented startTransition async caveat, how should the state update after await remain marked as a Transition?
questions.correctAnswer: Wrap the post-await setter in another startTransition: startTransition(() => setResult(data));
questions.explanation:
1. The initial transition context does not automatically mark this post-await setter under the documented limitation.
2. Await resumes later.
3. Explicitly marking the update preserves its scheduling intent. Handle request ordering separately.
hints: An await creates an asynchronous boundary.
Which setter needs its own marking?

questions.question: How does useDeferredValue differ from debouncing search requests?
questions.correctAnswer: It lets a dependent UI lag behind a newer value during rendering. It does not impose a fixed delay. It does not by itself prevent a network request for every keystroke.
questions.explanation: Deferring render priority and reducing request frequency solve different problems. Use a request policy separately when request volume matters.
hints: Scheduling is not a timer policy.
What actually starts the network request?

questions.question: Write Search({ items }) using urgent query state and a deferred query for a memoized result list. Items have stable id and name fields.
questions.explanation:
1. Typing updates query urgently.
2. Results can keep the previous deferred query while background rendering proceeds.
3. Memoization helps skip the unchanged result props; items identity should remain stable. Filtering remains O(n).
hints: Keep two render priorities for the same input.
Which query should the result list receive?

questions.question: What is the relationship between useOptimistic’s base value and its optimistic updates?
questions.correctAnswer: The base value is the authoritative state supplied to the Hook. Optimistic updates temporarily derive a pending view from it. When the Action completes, reconcile with the authoritative result rather than treating the optimistic view as confirmed storage.
questions.explanation: Optimism changes perceived latency, not server truth. The update function must remain pure so React can recompute the optimistic view when the base changes.
hints: Separate pending intent from confirmed state.
Which value comes from the successful mutation?

questions.question: What is unsafe about this useOptimistic reducer, and what expression should replace its body?
questions.correctAnswer: It mutates the supplied state. Return a new array: return [...state, message];
questions.explanation:
1. push edits the base array in place.
2. Reusing that array corrupts the distinction between authoritative and optimistic state.
3. A pure return value can be recalculated safely.
hints: Optimistic calculations are still pure.
Can the original array remain untouched?

questions.question: Which tuple does useActionState return?
questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: The Hook manages the latest action result, an action dispatcher and pending state. It does not return an Effect cleanup function or a mutable ref.
hints: Think state, action, progress.
Which member submits the next action?

questions.question: Why is formData.get failing after wiring save to useActionState?
questions.explanation:
1. useActionState prepends the current state to the action arguments.
2. The single parameter therefore receives state, not FormData.
3. Read the form payload from the second parameter; return the next state.
hints: Check the wrapped action signature.
Which argument does the Hook add?

questions.question: Write a complete NameForm using useActionState. Its action trims a submitted name and returns it locally; no network is needed.
questions.explanation:
1. The form supplies FormData to the action dispatcher.
2. save receives previous state first and returns the new state.
3. The Hook exposes the result and pending status. Client validation is not server authorization.
hints: Return the next state from the action.
Use the dispatcher as the form action.

questions.question: Why does useFormStatus usually belong in a SubmitButton rendered inside the form?
questions.correctAnswer: It reads the status of a parent form. It does not observe a form returned later by the same component. Put the consumer below the form whose submission it should track.
questions.explanation: Hook lookup follows the rendered ancestry. A component cannot read a descendant form’s status merely because it creates that JSX.
hints: The form must be an ancestor.
Where is the Hook relative to the form?

questions.question: Which statement about React’s use API is correct?

options.text: Every Hook can now be called conditionally.
use is valid in arbitrary event handlers.
A try/catch around use is the recommended loading boundary.
use can be called in conditions and loops, but still from a component or Hook.

questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: use is an exception to ordinary Hook ordering restrictions. It must not be wrapped in try/catch for promise suspension; use Suspense and error boundaries.
hints: This API has special call rules.
Which restrictions remain despite conditional calls?

questions.question: A client component creates a new fetch promise during every render and passes it to use. What should change?
questions.correctAnswer: Provide a stable promise from a supported cache or framework integration. A Server Component can also create and pass a promise to a Client Component. Recreating uncached promises during client rendering can repeatedly suspend.
questions.explanation: A promise is a resource identity, not just a value container. use does not automatically turn arbitrary fresh requests into a deduplicated data cache.
hints: Track promise identity across retries.
Can the same pending resource be reused?

questions.question: How does use handle a rejected promise during rendering?
questions.correctAnswer: It propagates the rejection to the nearest error boundary. Pending promises activate Suspense. To provide an alternate value, transform the promise with catch before passing it to use.
questions.explanation: A Suspense fallback represents waiting rather than a complete error recovery policy. Wrapping use in try/catch is not the supported boundary mechanism.
hints: Pending and rejected are different states.
Which boundary handles a rendering failure?

questions.question: Does placing two overlapping search requests in startTransition ensure the newest request’s result wins?
questions.correctAnswer: No, request completion can occur out of order. Use an ordering strategy or a framework Action abstraction with the required guarantees. Cancellation or request IDs can prevent obsolete results from committing.
questions.explanation: Scheduling priority does not establish network order. A slow older request can still resolve after a newer request without explicit coordination.
hints: Priority and causality differ.
Which response is still relevant?

questions.question: What does React Compiler automate, and what coding rules still matter?
questions.correctAnswer: It can automatically memoize eligible component computations and values. Components and Hooks must still follow React’s purity and Hook rules. Use profiling and compiler diagnostics rather than adding manual memoization everywhere.
questions.explanation: Compilation is a performance tool, not permission to mutate render inputs. It also does not remove network latency or replace application architecture.
hints: Automation depends on analyzable semantics.
Which React rules let work be reused safely?

questions.question: A team enables React Compiler. Should it immediately remove every existing useMemo and useCallback?
questions.correctAnswer: Avoid a blanket cleanup without evidence. Verify compiler coverage and behavior first. Remove unnecessary manual caching deliberately, with performance checks where it mattered.
questions.explanation: Existing manual memoization can document assumptions or interact with uncompiled code. Compiler adoption is not proof that every cache is irrelevant.
hints: Adoption coverage may be partial.
Which components are actually compiled?

questions.question: Design context usage for stable account identity and rapidly changing cursor coordinates. What split avoids unnecessary account-consumer updates?
questions.correctAnswer: Use separate contexts or a suitable store for independently changing data. Keep account consumers subscribed only to account data. Place high-frequency cursor updates close to the UI that needs them.
questions.explanation: One combined provider value couples consumers to unrelated updates. memo cannot shield a component from context it actually consumes.
hints: Separate update frequencies.
Which consumers need cursor changes?

questions.question: What must the client’s initial render match when hydrating server HTML?
questions.correctAnswer: It must describe the same initial content as the server output. Differences should be treated as bugs. Browser-only changes can be applied after hydration through a deliberate client lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Hydration attaches React behavior to existing markup. It is not a guaranteed general-purpose patcher for arbitrary server/client disagreement.
hints: Compare initial renders.
Did time, randomness or locale change the markup?

questions.question: Why can this ID cause hydration problems, and what should replace its generation?
questions.explanation:
1. The server generates one random ID.
2. The client’s first render generates another.
3. A coordinated ID avoids mismatched attributes; data keys should still come from data rather than useId.
hints: The first two renders must agree.
Which React API coordinates relationship IDs?

questions.question: An Effect connects by roomId but should log with the latest theme without reconnecting on theme changes. What does useEffectEvent offer?
questions.correctAnswer: Move the nonreactive logging behavior into an Effect Event. It can read the latest values when called from the Effect. Keep roomId as a real Effect dependency and do not use this API to hide required dependencies.
questions.explanation: Effect Events separate nonreactive logic from synchronization triggers. They are not general callbacks to pass around or invoke from arbitrary event handlers.
hints: Separate the reconnect trigger from latest-value reads.
Which value should change the subscription?

questions.question: What is the purpose of React’s Activity boundary when its mode becomes hidden?
questions.correctAnswer: It can preserve a subtree’s state while hiding its UI. Its Effects are cleaned up while hidden. When visible again, Effects are recreated with the preserved state.
questions.explanation: Keeping state is different from keeping every external subscription active. Activity is not simply an unconditional guarantee that all hidden work continues normally.
hints: State and Effects have different lifecycles.
Which resources should pause while hidden?

questions.question: Which mechanism can help avoid replacing already revealed content with a fallback during a non-urgent update?

options.text: Mark the relevant update as a Transition.
Use a random key on every render.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: Transitions can keep revealed content visible while new content prepares. Newly introduced boundaries and urgent updates still have their own fallback behavior.
hints: Preserve useful content during waiting.
Is the update urgent?

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-078: what should happen when the server rejects an optimistic edit?
questions.correctAnswer: Reconcile back to confirmed state or present an explicit recoverable failure. Explain the failure near the affected action. Preserve retryable user input when appropriate rather than claiming the edit succeeded.
questions.explanation: Optimistic rendering is provisional. A pending view must not become authoritative merely because it was displayed first.
hints: An optimistic result is not confirmation.
What data is still known to be correct?

questions.question: For a shareable search page, how should URL filters, a temporary open dropdown and server results be owned?
questions.correctAnswer: Keep shareable filters in the routing or URL state model. Keep transient dropdown visibility local. Let the data layer own fetched results and derive views from those sources.
questions.explanation: Duplicating each value into several independent stores creates synchronization problems. State structure should reflect persistence, sharing and ownership requirements.
hints: Different values have different lifetimes.
Which state must survive a shared link?

questions.question: A Profiler reports high render duration for a list. What should be checked before introducing memoization?
questions.correctAnswer: Confirm the slow interaction in a representative build. Inspect component work, state placement and changing props. Apply an optimization to the measured bottleneck and compare the result.
questions.explanation: Memoization can help repeated unchanged work but not every source of latency. Development diagnostics and profiling overhead can affect measurements.
hints: Measure the actual interaction.
Which computation consumes the time?

questions.question: Follow-up to REACT-052: should a modal expose open() when its visibility can be expressed with an isOpen prop?
questions.correctAnswer: Prefer an isOpen prop for declarative visibility. Reserve an imperative handle for operations such as focus that genuinely require it. A clear ownership model prevents parent and child visibility state from drifting.
questions.explanation: Imperative handles are an escape hatch. Exposing more methods does not automatically make a component easier to coordinate.
hints: Ask who owns visibility.
Can a prop describe the desired state?

questions.question: Design loading, error and optimistic states for a saveable editor without treating them as one boolean.
questions.correctAnswer: Track authoritative data and local draft separately. Represent pending submission and optimistic presentation explicitly. Use loading boundaries for suspended reads and error handling appropriate to failed reads or writes.
questions.explanation: A single loading flag cannot distinguish initial loading, background refresh and failed mutation. Clear state ownership prevents a failed save from silently discarding a valid draft.
hints: List independent state dimensions.
Can loading and an existing draft coexist?

questions.question: Which type requires narrowing before arbitrary property access?
questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.explanation: unknown safely represents an unvalidated value. any disables ordinary checking for its uses and can spread unchecked operations through the code.
hints: Look for a checked top type.
Which type forces proof before use?

questions.question: Under strictNullChecks, why is this unsafe, and what expression returns zero when the name is absent?
questions.correctAnswer: name may be undefined. Use: return name?.length ?? 0;
questions.explanation:
1. The optional parameter includes undefined.
2. Direct length access has no guarantee of a string.
3. Optional access plus a nullish fallback handles absence while preserving a real length of zero.
hints: The parameter is optional.
Narrow or guard before property access.

questions.question: Why can a value with extra fields often be assigned to an interface that requires only id and name?
questions.correctAnswer: TypeScript generally checks structural compatibility. The value must provide the required members with compatible types. Fresh object literals receive additional excess-property checks in certain assignment contexts.
questions.explanation: Types are not nominal class identities by default. Excess-property checks are a useful literal check, not a universal exact-object-type guarantee.
hints: Compare shapes, not declarations.
Is this a fresh literal or an existing variable?

questions.question: For value: string | number, which operation is valid without first narrowing?
questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation: Both members support toString. String-only and number-only methods need narrowing before they can be called safely.
hints: Use the common member set.
Which method exists on both alternatives?

questions.question: Write format(value: string | number): string, uppercasing strings and formatting numbers with two decimals.
questions.explanation:
1. typeof narrows the first branch to string.
2. The remaining branch is number.
3. Each branch uses a valid method and returns a string; no assertion is needed.
hints: Use a runtime type test.
What remains after the string branch returns?

questions.question: What does never represent, and how can it help with exhaustiveness?
questions.correctAnswer: never represents values that cannot occur. A fully handled union can narrow to never. Assigning an unhandled variant to never reveals a missing case at compile time.
questions.explanation: never is not equivalent to unknown or void. It models impossibility, while void describes an ignored or absent meaningful return value.
hints: Think of an empty set of values.
What type should remain after every case is handled?

questions.question: Why does this assertion not prove the API response has a name?
questions.explanation:
1. The network can return any JSON value.
2. as User only changes the compiler’s view.
3. A missing name can still fail at runtime; use real checks or a schema validator at the boundary.
hints: Compilation does not inspect future JSON.
What JavaScript does the assertion emit?

questions.question: What does as const do to this object’s mode property at the type level?
questions.code: const settings = { mode: "dark" } as const;

options.text: It becomes readonly with the literal type "dark".

questions.correctAnswer: D
questions.explanation:
1. TypeScript sees a const assertion on the object literal.
2. It retains the literal "dark" type and marks the property readonly in the inferred type.
3. The assertion emits no runtime freezing, so this is a static restriction rather than Object.freeze.
hints: Separate static typing from runtime freezing.
Does the type stay a specific literal?

questions.question: What does ReadonlyArray<T> prevent, and what does it not guarantee?
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents mutation through that typed array reference. It does not freeze the runtime array. Mutable aliases and mutable element objects can still change underlying data.
questions.explanation: readonly is a compile-time access restriction. Deep immutability and ownership require additional design beyond a readonly array annotation.
hints: Follow aliases to the same object.
Are the elements themselves immutable?

questions.question: Write greet(name?: string): string returning Hello, Guest only when name is undefined. Preserve an empty string.
questions.explanation:
1. The optional parameter includes undefined.
2. The nullish operator chooses Guest only for absence in this type domain.
3. An empty string is preserved, unlike with ||.
hints: Absence and empty text differ.
Which fallback preserves falsy strings?

questions.question: Follow-up to TS-001: why prefer unknown over any for an unvalidated parsed payload?
questions.correctAnswer: It forces consumers to establish the shape before use. Narrowing documents that proof. any would allow unchecked operations to spread beyond the boundary.
questions.explanation: unknown is not validation by itself. Runtime checks are still needed, but the type system requires them before unsafe property access.
hints: Make uncertainty visible.
Which operations should require evidence?

questions.question: Implement identity<T>(value: T): T without assertions or any.
questions.explanation:
1. The type parameter captures the caller’s input type.
2. The return uses the same type parameter.
3. Returning unknown would lose the input/output relationship, while any would skip checking.
hints: Relate input and output with one parameter.
No conversion is required.

questions.question: Implement getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(object: T, key: K): T[K].
questions.explanation:
1. keyof T limits keys to the object’s known property keys.
2. K preserves the specific chosen key.
3. T[K] returns that property’s type instead of a broad union.
hints: Constrain the key using the object type.
How do you index a type by a key?

questions.question: For T extends { length: number }, what can the generic function safely assume?

options.text: T must be an array of numbers.
Every accepted T has a numeric length property.
T has no properties other than length.
T can be accessed as any without checking.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.explanation: A constraint guarantees required structure without discarding additional information from T. It does not restrict T to arrays or make every property available.
hints: A constraint is a minimum shape.
Could a string also satisfy it?

questions.question: The function must preserve empty strings. What narrowing condition should replace the truthiness check?
questions.correctAnswer: Use: if (value !== null) { return value; }
questions.explanation:
1. The union is string or null.
2. A truthiness check rejects both null and the empty string.
3. Explicit null comparison narrows to string while preserving valid empty input.
hints: Falsy is broader than null.
Which one union member should be excluded?

questions.question: Write readResult(result: Result): string for the shown union, returning data on success and error on failure.
questions.explanation:
1. The literal ok property distinguishes union members.
2. The true branch exposes data.
3. The false branch exposes error; optional fields on one broad interface would weaken that relationship.
hints: Use the shared discriminant.
Which fields exist in each branch?

questions.question: What responsibility does a function returning value is User take on?
questions.correctAnswer: It promises that a true result proves the User shape. TypeScript uses that promise to narrow callers. The function must perform sufficient runtime checks because an incorrect predicate can make later code unsafe.
questions.explanation: The compiler does not derive every declared predicate’s truth from its implementation. A type predicate is a contract, not automatic schema validation.
hints: A predicate is trusted evidence.
Does its implementation check every required field?

questions.question: Write isUser(value: unknown): value is User for User = { name: string }.
questions.code:
type User = { name: string };
// Implement isUser(value: unknown): value is User.
questions.explanation:
1. Exclude primitives and null.
2. Check that name exists before reading its type.
3. The string test establishes the required shape. This structural guard permits extra properties and inherited name properties by contract.
hints: Narrow before accessing a field.
Remember typeof null is object.

questions.question: What does Partial<User> change?

options.text: It makes every nested field optional recursively.
It makes each top-level User property optional.
It returns a runtime proxy for User.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: Partial is a mapped utility over the top-level keys. It does not recursively make nested properties optional or validate patches at runtime.
hints: Consider the depth of the transformation.
Does it recurse into object fields?

questions.question: Define PublicUser from User, retaining only id and name, using a utility type.
questions.code:
type User = { id: string; name: string; passwordHash: string };
// Define PublicUser.
questions.correctAnswer:
type User = { id: string; name: string; passwordHash: string };
type PublicUser = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;
questions.explanation:
1. Pick selects the named properties at the type level.
2. The resulting type describes only the public fields.
3. It does not remove passwordHash from an existing runtime object; actual serialization needs a projection.
hints: Select a subset of keys.
Types do not strip runtime data.

questions.question: Why use satisfies for a configuration object instead of annotating the variable with a broad Record type?
questions.correctAnswer: It checks assignability to the required shape. It can preserve useful specific inferred property types. It does not cast an incompatible value into validity or perform runtime validation.
questions.explanation: An annotation can widen the accessible type to the annotated contract. satisfies still supplies contextual typing, so it is not a promise that inference is completely unaffected.
hints: Separate checking from replacing the variable’s type.
Which property-specific operations should remain available?

questions.question: Why does combine accept one or three arguments but reject two, despite optional implementation parameters?
questions.correctAnswer:
The implementation signature is not callable by consumers. If two arguments are intended, add this public overload before the implementation.

function combine(a: string, b: string): string;
questions.explanation:
1. Callers are checked against declared overloads.
2. The implementation signature exists to implement them and is not an additional callable overload.
3. Optional implementation parameters do not automatically expose every arity.
hints: Separate public overloads from implementation.
Which signatures can callers see?

questions.question: Write a typed Button accepting normal button props plus a required label. Use ComponentPropsWithoutRef.
questions.explanation:
1. Derive the native element prop contract.
2. Remove label before spreading DOM props.
3. The wrapper keeps native event and disabled typing; this specific API intentionally does not expose a ref.
hints: Reuse React’s element prop types.
Which custom prop must stay off the DOM node?

questions.question: Write handleChange(event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>): void that logs the current input value.
questions.code:
// .tsx usage contract; implement handleChange with a typed input event.
const field = <input onChange={handleChange} />;
questions.explanation:
1. The generic event type identifies the input element.
2. currentTarget is the element owning the handler.
3. Its value is a string; number inputs still need explicit conversion when numeric data is required.
hints: Tie the event to the element type.
Which target is guaranteed to own this handler?

questions.question: Why can adding a User fail here, and what explicit Hook type fixes it?
questions.correctAnswer: An empty array can infer an unusably narrow element type. Use: const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
questions.explanation:
1. The initializer contains no User element for inference.
2. The explicit generic supplies the intended array element type.
3. Future updates are then checked against User rather than requiring unsafe assertions.
hints: The initializer provides no element evidence.
Specify the intended state domain.

questions.question: What changes when strictNullChecks is enabled?
questions.correctAnswer: null and undefined are treated as distinct types. Potentially absent values must be handled before use where a definite value is required. This makes absence part of the checked contract.
questions.explanation: The option does not add runtime checks. A non-null assertion can silence the compiler without making an absent value safe.
hints: Absence becomes explicit in types.
Who performs the runtime guard?

questions.question: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled, what is the type of values[index] for values: string[] and arbitrary numeric index?
questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.explanation: An arbitrary index may be out of bounds. The option adds undefined to unchecked indexed access rather than assuming every numeric index exists.
hints: Arrays can have missing indexes.
Is this index proven in range?

questions.question: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, how should a type-only User import be written?
questions.correctAnswer: Use: import type { User } from "./types";
questions.explanation:
1. The declaration is used only in type positions.
2. import type explicitly marks it for erasure.
3. A normal import is preserved according to verbatimModuleSyntax rules and can require an actual runtime export.

questions.question: Why may a function returning a value be assigned to a callback type returning void?
questions.correctAnswer: A contextual void return means the caller ignores the returned value. It does not necessarily forbid the implementation from producing one. Callers typed with that contract cannot use the value as a meaningful result.
questions.explanation: This rule supports callbacks such as array operations that discard results. It differs from explicitly declaring a function body with an incompatible annotated return.
hints: Think about what the caller promises to use.
Is the return discarded?

questions.question: A helper returns Promise<PromiseLike<User>> in its declared type. Which utility models the value obtained by awaiting it?
questions.correctAnswer: Use Awaited on the return type. It recursively unwraps promise-like values. Combine it with ReturnType when deriving the result from a function declaration.
questions.explanation: A single indexed access into a Promise type does not model await semantics. Awaited also distributes appropriately across supported unions.

questions.question: For type Wrap<T> = T extends string ? T[] : never, what is Wrap<"a" | "b">?

questions.explanation:

2. The conditional evaluates "a" and "b" separately, producing "a"[] and "b"[].

questions.question: How can template-literal types constrain event names such as user:created and user:deleted?
questions.correctAnswer: Combine literal unions inside a template-literal type. TypeScript expands the allowed combinations. Prefer generated declarations or runtime validation when the possible set becomes very large or comes from external input.
questions.explanation: The type restricts compile-time assignments but does not validate arbitrary runtime strings. Large cross-products can also increase type-checking cost.
hints: Build strings from finite pieces.

questions.question: When should a function prefer a union parameter over multiple overloads?
questions.correctAnswer: Prefer a union when the same operation and return type handle all accepted inputs. Use overloads when distinct call signatures express meaningful input/output relationships. Keep the public API as simple as its contract allows.
questions.explanation: Overloads can reject a union-valued argument even when each individual overload accepts one member. More overloads are not automatically more precise for callers.
hints: Look for relationships, not just alternatives.
Does the return type depend on the input shape?

questions.question: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled, how can this API explicitly allow assigning undefined as well as omission?

const options: Options = { theme: undefined };
questions.correctAnswer: Include undefined explicitly: type Options = { theme?: "dark" | "light" | undefined };
questions.explanation:

2. With exact optional semantics, it does not automatically permit writing undefined unless declared.
3. Add the union only if explicit undefined is part of the API contract.
hints: Omission differs from a present undefined property.

questions.question: A component accepts either { kind: "link", href } or { kind: "button", onClick }. Why is a discriminated union better than making href and onClick optional on one type?
questions.correctAnswer: It expresses which fields are required for each mode. Invalid combinations can be rejected statically. Narrowing kind gives the implementation access to the correct fields.
questions.explanation: Independent optional properties allow states such as a link with no href. The type should encode the real component contract instead of requiring repeated defensive assumptions.
hints: Model valid combinations.
Which fields depend on the selected mode?

questions.question: Why type a DOM ref as HTMLInputElement | null?
questions.correctAnswer: The node is absent before it is attached. It can become absent again when removed. Nullability forces imperative consumers to handle those lifecycle states.
questions.explanation: A non-null assertion does not cause a node to exist. Event-time optional access or a suitable guard matches the actual lifecycle.

questions.question: Follow-up to TS-021: does satisfies make a downloaded configuration trustworthy at runtime?
questions.correctAnswer: No, it is a compile-time check. External data still needs runtime validation. Treat the parsed value as unknown until its required shape is established.
questions.explanation: Type-level operators are erased from emitted JavaScript. They cannot inspect data arriving after the program is built.
